name: Melanoma
overview: Melanoma is an aggressive form of skin cancer that develops from melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin. Although it accounts for a smaller proportion of skin cancer cases than basal cell carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma is responsible for the majority of skin cancer-related deaths because of its ability to spread (metastasize) to distant organs. Early recognition and treatment greatly improve outcomes.
description: Melanoma may arise within an existing mole or develop as a completely new pigmented lesion. It commonly appears on the back in men and on the legs in women but can occur anywhere on the body, including areas not regularly exposed to sunlight. Lesions often change over time in size, color, or shape. Early diagnosis followed by prompt surgical treatment offers the best chance of cure.
clinical_presentation: Multiple colors within the same lesion
Dark brown, black, blue, red, pink, or white pigmentation
Elevated or nodular appearance in some subtypes
Possible ulceration or bleeding in advanced lesions
typical_features: May develop itching, tenderness, or bleeding

ABCDE.Asymmetry: One half does not resemble the other half.
ABCDE.Border: Irregular, ragged, blurred, or poorly defined.
ABCDE.Color: Multiple shades including brown, black, blue, red, white, or pink.
ABCDE.Diameter: Often greater than 6 mm, although smaller melanomas can occur.
ABCDE.Evolution: Any change in size, shape, color, elevation, or symptoms should prompt immediate medical evaluation.

diagnostic_workup: Sentinel lymph node biopsy when clinically indicated
Imaging studies for staging in selected patients
treatment_options: Sentinel lymph node biopsy when indicated
prognosis: The prognosis depends primarily on the stage at diagnosis. Thin melanomas detected early are often curable with surgery alone. More advanced disease carries a higher risk of recurrence and metastasis, although modern immunotherapy and targeted treatments have substantially improved outcomes for many patients.
prevention: Follow the ABCDE rule when monitoring moles
Attend routine dermatology examinations if at increased risk
next_steps: Arrange urgent evaluation by a dermatologist.
An excisional biopsy is generally recommended to establish a definitive diagnosis.
Avoid attempting to remove or treat the lesion yourself.
Take dated clinical photographs to monitor changes while awaiting specialist assessment.
Follow all recommendations provided by your treating dermatologist.
red_flags: Satellite lesions near the primary lesion

follow_up.routine: Follow-up frequency depends on the stage of disease and should be determined by the treating dermatologist or oncology team.
follow_up.high_risk: Patients with confirmed melanoma generally require long-term dermatology surveillance and individualized follow-up planning.

patient_advice: Do not ignore a mole that is changing in appearance.
Monitor your skin using the ABCDE rule.
Seek prompt medical evaluation for any suspicious lesion.
Avoid excessive ultraviolet exposure and tanning beds.
Continue regular skin examinations even after treatment because new melanomas can develop.
